name: DC BLOX Myrtle Beach Cable Landing Station

profile.reading:
Per DC BLOX's own site, this Myrtle Beach, South Carolina cable landing station and data center sits at 1401 Howard Road and currently operates 40,000 square feet, designed for expansion up to 125,000 square feet, with 19 MW of power capacity committed and planned across two data centers, one operational and one in development. The facility is built to withstand sustained hurricane winds of 170 mph using pre-cast construction, runs 2N power generation, UPS, and switchgear with indirect adiabatic and evaporative N+1 cooling, and holds Uptime Institute Tier III concurrently maintainable design certification plus SOC 2 Type II compliance. The operator's own page states a 100 percent service level agreement covering power, temperature, and humidity, along with round-the-clock security and CCTV monitoring.

As a subsea cable landing station, the site can host up to 5 cables, with 3 announced as of the operator's own page connecting to 5 international locations, across 72 cable pairs. It connects via a high-capacity dark fiber route running from Lithia Springs, Georgia to Myrtle Beach, with direct links to Atlanta's internet exchanges and a dark fiber metro ring planned around Atlanta. This positions the facility as an East Coast subsea gateway distinct from DC BLOX's inland Southeast colocation sites like Birmingham and Chattanooga, tracked elsewhere in this registry.

DC BLOX operates a network of data centers across the Southeast United States. Per the company's own data center map page, it operates 23 facilities totaling 2,780,376 square feet and 470 critical MW company-wide, a company-level aggregate this registry does not apply to this individual facility's own figures above. No year-opened date was located in sourcing reachable for this row. No public ownership structure or investor detail specific to DC BLOX was located in sourcing reachable for this row. DC BLOX positions itself as a regional Southeast US colocation and network fabric provider rather than a national hyperscale operator, and this Myrtle Beach site's subsea cable landing role gives the company a distinctive coastal gateway function alongside its inland colocation facilities in markets like Birmingham, Chattanooga, and Huntsville, a strategy distinct from the dense Northern Virginia or Silicon Valley clustering seen among many other operators tracked in this registry.

reading.body:
This Myrtle Beach facility operates 19 MW of IT capacity in 40,000 square feet of current technical space, with design capacity for expansion to 125,000 square feet. Assuming typical AI training density of 40 kW per rack, 19 MW of IT load translates to roughly 475 racks. The facility is built to Uptime Institute Tier III concurrently maintainable design and holds SOC 2 Type II compliance, qualifying it to host colocation and compliance-sensitive workloads. It runs 2N power generation with indirect adiabatic and evaporative N+1 cooling, and is hardened against sustained hurricane winds of 170 mph.

The site functions as an East Coast subsea cable landing station, equipped to host up to 5 transatlantic and international cables across 72 cable pairs, with 3 cables announced as of the operator's page. It connects via dark fiber to Lithia Springs, Georgia and Atlanta's internet exchanges, positioning it as a gateway for international traffic distinct from DC BLOX's inland Southeast colocation sites. This subsea function places the facility in a narrower class than hyperscale compute campuses, optimizing for network ingress and compliance workloads rather than dense AI training.

In South Carolina, this facility ranks fifth by published megawatts among 14 mapped data centers in the state, and is one of only 4 sites that publish capacity figures. South Carolina's total published capacity stands at 6.6 MW across those four facilities. The operator does not publish a year-opened date for this site. The operator's company-wide figure of 470 MW across 23 facilities does not apply to individual facility planning.
